newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 29.

text.p: THE DOMINION

A fully staffed million-dollar centre to get former women prisoners off alcohol and drugs is to stay empty for nearly three months while it is decided if the programme is working. The 10-patient unit at Plimmerton, north of Wellington, has seven staff, with around-the-clock supervisors, even though it has no patients. Page 1.

A marathon session on Maori affairs for NZ First and National negotiators on Thursday threw coalition talks off schedule, forcing the postponement of a session with Labour. Maori issues have always been a big area of difference between National and NZ First, and Thursday's session lasted more than four hours. NZ First wants National to scrap its $1 billion "fiscal envelope" cap on Treaty of Waitangi settlements and, driven by its five Maori electorate MPs, is seeking a wide range of concessions is other areas of Maori policy. Informal negotiations continue on Friday and contacts are expected during the weekend, though many NZ First MPs will be in Peters'
Tauranga electorate for a Sunday rally. Page 1.

Australia's bitter debate on immigration took a new turn on Wednesday when an ethnic forum in Townsville was told Australians should be more concerned about New Zealand immigrants than about Asians. Federal Immigration and Multicultural Affairs Minister Philip Ruddock said New Zealand immigrants were more highly represented in Australian jails and hospitals than their Asian counterparts. Page 2.

NZ First's compulsory savings policy needs "a huge amount of work" to turn it into a workable pension scheme, according to insurance company Prudential. Prudential general manager Anthony Molloy issued the company's analysis of NZ First's policy on Thursday, saying it lacked so much detail that it provided more questions than answers. Page 2.

Maori who do not know their tribal links have been urged to find out or risk missing out on benefiting from Maori fisheries assets. The Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission, which holds several hundred million dollars worth of assets on behalf of
Maoridom, has set up a free "iwi helpline" to help people establish their roots. Page 2.

The economy is slowing considerably and a recession is emerging in the export and import competing sectors, according to Wellington economists Berl in its November forecasts. Berl says it is not being pessimistic, but is the first to recognise fully the scale of the effects of tight monetary policies with a high exchange rate and high interest rates. The Wellington Manufacturers Association said on Thursday unless there was rapid action of the exchange rate, exports would keep plummeting
and the record trade deficit would "accelerate beyond control". Page 17.
The New Zealand Government still has quality assets, such as airports, that could be sold, according to Jonathon Davie, deputy chairman of international merchant bank BZW. Page 17.

Business confidence has rebounded from its pre-election jitters, according to the National Bank's latest monthly survey. All sectors were more confident this month than they were in October, but especially in service companies and retail traders.
Page 17.

The New Zealand dollar has been about three percent to five percent overvalued against the Australian dollar, according to a study by the National Bank. That suggested a fair value of around A87 cents to the New Zealand dollar, National Bank said. The dollar was down to A87.44 cents on Thursday, from about A90 cents earlier this month. Page 17.

Lion Nathan on Thursday signalled a further change in senior management with the announcement that Kevin Roberts would step down as chief operating officer in February and not be replaced. The group has recently reported several management changes. Thursday's news was greeted negatively in the sharemarket in view of Roberts' important role in Lion's expansion into Australia and China and its Pepsi development. Page 17.

Failing political leadership risked sending New Zealand back into a worsening economy and "borrow and hope" policies, Business Roundtable chief executive Douglas Myers said on Thursday. He was particularly critical of National and Prime Minister Jim Bolger, and called on the business community to pressure politicians for further reforms and better policy. Page 18.
Economists say the forecasts in Monday's December economic and fiscal update by Treasury could be out of date within days and that the document is based on unrealistic assumptions. Page 18.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

An Appeal Court judge has taken judges to task for the way they treat some rape complaints. Justice Thomas has criticised the "recent complaint rule", which says some evidence may not be admissible if a woman delayed in telling anyone about the alleged rape.
Bosses of the 23 crown health enterprises were paid bonuses of up to $34,000 last financial year, despite some failing to keep within budget.

NZ First MPs are heading to Tauranga this weekend for a retreat as the tandem talks on the coalition gain pace and decision-day nears. The retreat coincides with a public rally that the leader Winston Peters and other Bay of Plenty MPs will hold in Tauranga on Sunday.

The Business Roundtable has warned of "cop-out" politicians who see MMP as an excuse to halt change. The table chairman Doug Myers told Auckland business leaders on Thursday that the early signs from the coalition talks were not good. It appeared all four key economic policies -- Labour law, free trade, less tax and low inflation -- were on the bargaining table.

Air New Zealand's capacity problems on Christmas season flights across the Tasman are spilling over to its budget airline, Freedom Air International. The subsidiary company announced on Thursday it was having to reschedule flights
affecting 1,000 passengers.

One of the driving forces in Lion Nathan's executive brew, Kevin Roberts, is calling it quits after eight years with the company. His forthright style as chief operating officer recently came under scrutiny following a number of defections from Lion's senior ranks in Australia.

Apple and Pear Board management are recommending Apple Field be given an export consent for only 37,000 cartons of apples, the Christchurch-based orchardist said on Thursday. It is seeking leave to export 1.5 million cartons independently of the board and has said it will quit the apple-growing business and subdivide the properties if it does not get it.
